sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax
sections.html:
The county does the work here. It sets the tax on land, buildings and mobile homes, collects it, and splits the money among itself, cities, townships, school districts and other local districts. The State Tax Commissioner publishes the calendar and oversees the state boards, yet your check goes to the county treasurer.

A bill is built from the mill rate, the taxable value and the taxing entity. Values are set as of February 1. Assessed value is 50 percent of market value, which is the price the property would bring if sold now. The county auditor builds the tax list and delivers it to the treasurer by December 10, and the treasurer must mail a statement by December 26.

Selling? Call the treasurer's office early and ask what is owed on the parcel, what is paid, and whether an older year is still open.

Real estate tax is due on January 1 following the year it was levied and becomes delinquent after March 1 for a single payment or the first installment. N.D.C.C. 57-20-01 adds a 3 percent penalty to an unpaid first installment after March 1, then another 3 percent on each of May 1, July 1 and October 15. The second installment becomes delinquent after October 15 and takes a 6 percent penalty.

DateWhat happens
January 1Tax for the prior levy year is due
February 15Pay the whole year's tax by this date for a 5 percent discount
March 1First installment is penalty-free through this day
October 15Second installment is penalty-free through this day
November 1Abatement applications for the earlier year's tax are due
December 26Treasurers mail the new tax statements

If a due date falls on a day the treasurer's office is closed, payment on the next open day carries no penalty and no loss of discount. A statement that never arrives is not an excuse. Failure to receive one does not relieve the owner or extend the February 15 discount deadline.

The county treasurer allows a 5 percent discount to taxpayers who pay all of a parcel's real estate tax for the year on or before February 15. It applies to general taxes for the state, county, city, township, school district and other districts. It does not apply to special assessment installments, and it is figured before the Primary Residence Credit.

  • A county commission can extend the discount period by 30 days if it finds a weather or other emergency.
  • Installments must be at least 10 percent of the tax and never less than $10.
  • No discount applies to payment on property that has delinquent tax.

Money paid on a parcel with older tax owed goes first to the oldest delinquent amount, along with its penalty and interest. A seller catching up before closing should expect the payment to be applied that way.

An owner can appeal through a chain of equalization boards that meet in a fixed order during spring and summer. The assessor must deliver written notice of the value at least 15 days before the local board meets, and the notice gives the dates of the local and county board meetings.

  • Township and city boards of equalization sit in April on locally chosen dates. Ask the county or city auditor for yours.
  • The county board meets during the first 10 days of June. Owners may appear personally, send a representative, or appeal by mail stating their reasons.
  • The State Board of Equalization takes up locally assessed property on the second Tuesday in August. Individuals can speak and submit written material or photographs. The Property Tax division takes questions at propertytax@nd.gov or 701-328-3127.

If you disagree with a bill after it is issued, two more routes exist. You can pay under protest to the county treasurer with written reasons, then apply to the county commissioners within 60 days for abatement, adjustment or a refund. The separate abatement application for an earlier year's tax is due by November 1.

sections.h2: Credits that lower a homeowner's bill
sections.html:
Three state credits can reduce what a homeowner owes. The Primary Residence Credit is up to $1,600 against the tax due, for an owner who lives in a house, mobile home, town home, duplex or condo as a primary residence, with no age or income limits. A homeowner can also hold the Homestead or Disabled Veteran's credit and still use the Primary Residence Credit on any remaining balance.

  • Primary Residence Credit: up to $1,600, never more than the tax due. Owner must live in the home, and applications open in January and close April 1.
  • Homestead Property Tax Credit: for owners age 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled, with income of $70,000 or less in the year before the assessment date.
  • Disabled Veteran's Property Tax Credit: cuts taxable value by up to $9,000 at a 100 percent rating, and moves with the owner to a new homestead.

These credits belong to the person living in the house. A buyer who moves in has to file a fresh application.

Tax left unpaid turns into a lien. After at least two years the county can foreclose and take the property by tax deed. Each year from November 1 to 15 the treasurer mails every delinquent owner a notice saying the tax is a lien, and that foreclosure will follow unless it is paid by October 1 of the second year after delinquency.

The auditor must give foreclosure notice by June 1. The foreclosure date is October 1 after service, and the tax deed then passes the property to the county free of most encumbrances. Section 57-28-04 adds foreclosure costs of $50 or actual costs, whichever is higher, to the amount needed to clear the lien. A residential property gets personal service by the sheriff if the owner lives in the state.

Tax deed land is appraised, then sold at auction starting the third Tuesday in November for cash or one-fourth down with the balance over up to ten years. While the county holds title, the former owner, the owner's executor, or a parent, spouse or child can buy the property back. Any sale money beyond the taxes and costs is held for 90 days so the record owner can claim it.

Whatever is owed, including penalty and interest, is deducted from the seller's proceeds at closing. The treasurer credits it to the oldest year first. The title company checks the treasurer's records for current and delinquent tax and for special assessments, which are billed with the tax.

Before you list or take an offer, run through these steps:

  • Get a payoff figure from the county treasurer ahead of closing.
  • Check the first and second installment status for the year, since the second is not delinquent until after October 15.
  • Ask whether any special assessment installments are outstanding.
  • For an inherited house, find out who got the tax statement, since only one owner at the last-known address receives it.

The purchase contract decides how this year's tax is divided between buyer and seller, so read that clause first. If a lien notice has already been mailed, speed matters, because the October 1 foreclosure date is fixed by statute. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, so the time between signing and payoff is shorter. The delinquent amount comes out of the proceeds and the lien clears at the closing table.

faqs.q: What is the North Dakota property tax due date?
faqs.a: The tax is due January 1 and goes delinquent after March 1. You may split it into two installments, the second penalty-free through October 15. Paying everything by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount.

faqs.q: What penalty applies to late North Dakota property tax?
faqs.a: A late first installment gets 3 percent after March 1 and another 3 percent on May 1, July 1 and October 15. A late second installment gets 6 percent after October 15.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my North Dakota property assessment?
faqs.a: Go first to the township or city board in April, next to the county board in early June, then to the State Board in August. The value notice is due to you at least 15 days before the local board sits.

faqs.q: How much is the North Dakota Primary Residence Credit?
faqs.a: It takes up to $1,600 off the tax due. There is no age or income test, but you must live in the home and apply by April 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in North Dakota if I owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is paid out of your proceeds at closing, oldest year first. Closing before the foreclosure date also keeps the county from taking the house by tax deed.
